{{Short description|Type of incidence structure}}
An [[incidence structure]] <math>C=(P,L,I)</math> consists of a set {{tmath|1= P }} of points, a set {{tmath|1= L }} of lines, and an incidence relation, or set of flags, <math>I \subseteq P \times L</math>; a point <math>p</math> is said to be ''incident'' with a line <math>l</math> if {{tmath|1= (p,l) \in I }}. It is a ([[Wikt:finite|finite]]) '''partial geometry''' if there are [[integer]]s <math>s,t,\alpha\geq 1</math> such that:
* For any pair of distinct points <math>p</math> and {{tmath|1= q }}, there is at most one line incident with both of them.
* Each line is incident with <math>s+1</math> points.
* Each point is incident with <math>t+1</math> lines.
* If a point <math>p</math> and a line <math>l</math> are not incident, there are exactly <math>\alpha</math> pairs {{tmath|1= (q,m)\in I}}, such that <math>p</math> is incident with <math>m</math> and <math>q</math> is incident with {{tmath|1= l }}.

A partial geometry with these parameters is denoted by {{tmath|1= \mathrm{pg}(s,t,\alpha) }}.

== Properties ==
* The number of points is given by <math>\frac{(s+1)(s t+\alpha)}{\alpha}</math> and the number of lines by {{tmath|1= \frac{(t+1)(s t+\alpha)}{\alpha} }}.
* The point graph (also known as the [[Collinearity#Collinearity graph|collinearity graph]]) of a <math>\mathrm{pg}(s,t,\alpha)</math> is a [[strongly regular graph]]: {{tmath|1= \mathrm{srg}\Big((s+1)\frac{(s t+\alpha)}{\alpha},s(t+1),s-1+t(\alpha-1),\alpha(t+1)\Big) }}.
* Partial geometries are dualizable structures: the dual of a <math>\mathrm{pg}(s,t,\alpha)</math> is simply a {{tmath|1= \mathrm{pg}(t,s,\alpha) }}.

== Special cases ==
* The [[generalized quadrangle]]s are exactly those partial geometries <math>\mathrm{pg}(s,t,\alpha)</math> with {{tmath|1= \alpha=1 }}.
* The [[Steiner system]]s <math>S(2, s+1, ts+1)</math> are precisely those partial geometries <math>\mathrm{pg}(s,t,\alpha)</math> with {{tmath|1= \alpha=s+1 }}.

== Generalisations ==
A [[partial linear space]] <math>S=(P,L,I)</math> of order <math>s, t</math> is called a '''semipartial geometry''' if there are [[integer]]s <math>\alpha\geq 1, \mu</math> such that:
* If a point <math>p</math> and a line <math>l</math> are not incident, there are either <math>0</math> or exactly <math>\alpha</math> pairs {{tmath|1= (q,m)\in I }}, such that <math>p</math> is incident with <math>m</math> and <math>q</math> is incident with {{tmath|1= l}}.
* Every pair of non-collinear points have exactly <math>\mu</math> common neighbours.

A semipartial geometry is a partial geometry if and only if {{tmath|1= \mu = \alpha(t+1) }}.

It can be easily shown that the collinearity graph of such a geometry is strongly regular with parameters 
{{tmath|1= (1 + s(t + 1) +  s(t+1)t(s - \alpha + 1)/\mu, s(t+1), s - 1 + t(\alpha - 1), \mu) }}.

A nice example of such a geometry is obtained by taking the affine points of <math>\mathrm{PG}(3, q^2)</math> and only those lines that intersect the plane at infinity in a point of a fixed Baer subplane; it has parameters {{tmath|1= (s, t, \alpha, \mu) = (q^2 - 1, q^2 + q, q, q(q + 1)) }}.
